# The Case for AI Guardrails: How We Switched AI from Copy-Pasta to Building the Way We Want

4 min read

*If a Rule is Not Encoded, It’s Not Enforceable*


Press enter or click to view image in full size


From “Took A Snap”


As we embraced AI agents creating code, we observed agents copying and pasting legacy patterns from our codebase into new pull requests. Our six-month, company-wide initiative on AI guardrails shows our approach to corralling these suboptimal patterns in our ever-expanding codebase.


*Six months of building guardrails for coding agents in a large Rails monolith*


## A Quick Win


In April 2025, we deprecated an internal job-enqueueing class and documented how to move off of it. Within a month, usage was down to 239 call sites. By December, the count was largely unchanged at 226. We’d successfully stopped that pattern from growing.


Then coding agents became part of everyday work, and by April 2026 the count was climbing again, up to 339. Nobody decided to reverse the migration. The agents saw 226 perfectly good working examples in the code, so they wrote more like them. The deprecation lived in a doc and in people’s heads, so agents couldn’t see it, and nothing enforced it.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


After a collective sigh, we followed a simple, repeatable pattern:


1. We added a lint rule that rejected new uses.
2. We used Claude extensively to remove the old ones.
3. The count went to zero, and this time it can’t come back, because both the pattern and the methods that allow it are gone. In this case, we don’t even need the deprecation linter anymore. We’ve rooted the pattern out.


That’s the idea behind our **AI Guardrails** initiative: **create rules that prevent agents from writing code patterns we don’t want.**


> *“Anything still in the codebase is something Claude will keep sampling from.” — Ben Golden, Gusto engineer, after finishing a long deprecation*


Every leftover example of an abandoned pattern works like a recommendation. At human speed, that debt was manageable. At agent speed, it spread like a galactic expansion.

## The Ratchet


We decided to call this solution a ‘ratchet,’ because just like a ratchet can only go in one direction, with this solution, violations can only go down. Each turn of the crank tightens things, and it only turns one way. Our linting ratchet has three parts:


1. **A list of rules that have known violations.** In our case, these are RuboCop cops that are disabled inline or listed in` .rubocop_todo.yml` .
2. **Removal-only ownership.** Anyone can make the list smaller. Adding to the list fails CI. Once you’ve fixed every violation of a rule, no new violations can appear.
3. **A coupling test** that keeps the todo file and the list of rules in agreement.


The list of partially followed rules peaked at 289 entries in February 2026 and has 157 today. Of the rules that had inline suppressions in March 2025, 123 now have none.

Over the same period, our custom rules grew from 77 to 193.


We also contributed the pattern upstream. RuboCop recently merged a` DisallowedCops` option ([rubocop/rubocop#15050](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/pull/15050) ). This implementation lets you manage the list easily, as new rules from upstream or local custom cops can be disabled automatically, and you don’t need to add an entry to this config each time. RuboCop and Shopify also changed the code so this rule has the highest priority and can't be disabled inline ([rubocop/rubocop#15512](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/pull/15512) ).


Since then, the “ratchet” has caught on at Gusto.


## Custom Guardrails Should Explain the Fix


When building custom rules, we’ve found it helpful to explain how to fix the problem in the error message. This points future AI agents in a desirable direction.


When a rule only says “no,” an AI agent can get clever and try to work around it.


For example, our rule against` sleep` in specs caps sleeps at 0.1 seconds and lists the fixes in order:


1. Delete it.
2. Assert on what you were waiting for.
3. Move the clock forward.
4. Trigger the state directly.
5. Only as a last resort, keep it with a written reason.


Following that guidance, we removed 76 sleeps, about 107 seconds of idle time per suite run. Removing them also turned up a few tests that weren’t asserting what they intended, and we tightened those up along the way. The rule now keeps that from happening again.


## Results


We’ve successfully gone from 117 unique RuboCop cops to 66 RuboCop cops. Periodically, we create new types of RuboCops to act as AI guardrails. When this happens, the graph will briefly go up.

## Your Turn


What do you keep catching in code review? Turn it into a rule.


When you deprecate something, use AI agents to aggressively delete the last examples, because agents will copy whatever is left.


Make the best path easy to find. Write rules that suggest their own fix. With RuboCop, that can be a check that runs in under a second, giving feedback both on the PR and before an agent pushes.


If a rule isn’t encoded, agents won’t (or can’t) reliably follow it. Give them a hand!
